prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm interested in Molds R Us, a small company that makes plastic moldings for houses in Russia. They want to know if investing in this company is a good idea. The firm also wants to understand what the 2011 market for moldings, particularly in plastics, will look like.
prompt.question: Should the PE firm invest in Molds R Us? The firm requires 20% revenue growth in the first year to justify the purchase. Please also estimate the size of the 2011 plastic moldings market in Russia.

clarifying_info.q: Does the PE firm want to expand this company beyond Russia?
clarifying_info.a: No. This company only plays in the Russian market and the PE firm is not interested in expanding across borders.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other competitors in plastic moldings?
clarifying_info.a: This company is the only player in plastic moldings.
Moldings are used where walls meet the ceiling to add decorative appeal to houses and are only used in residential buildings.

clarifying_info.q: Do all new housing starts require moldings?
clarifying_info.a: All housing starts require moldings in the year they are started, and all are completed by the next year.

exhibits.title: Types of Moldings
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of five molding options available in the Russian market, showing price per 10 meters, installation requirements, and replacement cycle for each type.

other_notes: A contractor can lay down 1000 feet of molding per hour
A contractor makes on average 50 Rubles per hour
The average house has 4000 Meters of walls

exhibits.title: Moldings Used in the Russian Market
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing the market share of each molding type (No Moldings, PVC Plastic, Rubber, Wood, Plaster) from 2005 to 2010, plus a table of total residences and housing starts for each year.

framework: Market attractiveness: size, growth rate, and competitive dynamics of the Russian plastic moldings market
Company assessment: Molds R Us competitive position, market share, and revenue base
Deal thesis validation: Can the PE firm achieve 20% year-one revenue growth?
Risks and next steps if the deal does not meet the threshold

questions.prompt: Estimate the number of meters of plastic moldings being sold in 2011.
questions.guidance: Candidate should project 2011 residences and housing starts by extrapolating 2010 trends, apply the 2010 plastic market share (~25%), account for the 5-year replacement cycle for existing homes, and multiply the resulting number of houses by 4,000 meters per house.

math.setup: 2011 total residences = 2010 residences + 2010 housing starts = 33.1M + 1.25M = 34.35M (approx 34.3M). Estimate 2011 housing starts by extrapolating ~30% annual growth: ~1.4M. Apply 25% plastic market share to existing residences; divide by 5 for replacement cycle. Apply 25% to new starts.
steps: Existing homes replacing moldings in 2011 (1/5 cycle): 8.6M / 5 = 1.72M (~1.7M)
Total homes buying plastic moldings in 2011: 1.7M + 0.35M = 2.05M
math.answer: Approximately 8.2 billion meters of plastic moldings will be sold in 2011.

questions.prompt: Calculate the overall market growth rate for plastic moldings from 2005 to 2010, and assess whether 20% first-year revenue growth is achievable.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that market growth has two components — existing home replacement demand (driven by overall residence growth, ~85% of market) and new housing starts (~15% of market). The stagnant plastic market share combined with low existing-home growth means overall growth will fall well short of 20%.

math.setup: Existing homes growth rate and new housing starts growth rate, weighted by their share of total demand.
steps: Existing homes CAGR: (33.1M - 29.7M) / 29.7M / 6 years = ~2% per year
New housing starts CAGR: (1.25M - 0.46M) / 0.46M / 6 years = ~30% per year
Existing homes are ~85% of plastic demand; new starts are ~15%
math.answer: Overall market growth is less than 10% (approximately 6%), well below the 20% threshold required by the PE firm.

brainstorming.prompt: If the PE firm still wanted to pursue growth opportunities, what alternatives or strategic levers could they consider?

categories.name: Adjacent product/material markets
ideas: Invest in a rubber moldings company, which has shown declining share but a still-meaningful base
Explore wood moldings, which has grown from 0% to 11% market share and shows the highest share growth trend

categories.name: Sales and marketing improvements at Molds R Us
ideas: Invest in marketing and distribution to convert the 45% of homes currently using no moldings
Expand sales channels to reach more contractors and DIY customers
Price competitively to gain share from rubber or wood alternatives

categories.name: Operational improvements
ideas: Improve contractor partnerships or training to reduce installation costs

categories.name: Market expansion (outside current PE mandate)
ideas: Expand to other CIS/Eastern European markets — noted as out of scope for this PE firm but a potential future angle

recommendation: The PE firm should NOT purchase Molds R Us.
Plastic molding market share has been stagnant at roughly 25-26% across all moldings sold from 2005-2010, with no upward trend.
Overall housing market growth (~2% for existing homes, ~30% for new starts) blended yields less than 10% market growth — well short of the required 20% first-year revenue growth threshold.
risks: If housing starts continue to accelerate, new-start-driven growth could be higher than modeled, but existing homes dominate the volume so the blended rate remains low.
Molds R Us has no pricing power signals in the data; revenue growth cannot easily be achieved through price increases in a price-competitive commodity market.
next_steps: The PE firm should evaluate rubber molding companies: rubber's market share has been high historically, and while declining, a well-run operator could capitalize on remaining demand.
Assess Molds R Us's sales and marketing capability to determine whether investment in distribution or marketing could convert the large 'no moldings' segment (45% in 2010) and spur growth.
If the PE firm reconsiders, model a scenario where plastic gains share from 'no moldings' households to stress-test the 20% growth target.
